name: FULL NETTLE JACKET BURGER (comes with sautéed nettles)

recipe.history:
Stinging nettles (Urtica dioica) are one of the most ancient and widespread wild food plants in human history, present on nearly every temperate continent and used as a food source by human populations for thousands of years before agriculture established more predictable alternatives. Archaeological evidence from Neolithic sites in Denmark and Switzerland indicates nettle seeds and fibers were collected routinely, and the plant's tender spring shoots were almost certainly eaten as a pot herb wherever they grew in abundance. In Britain the nettle has the longest continuous culinary history of perhaps any wild plant — Culpeper's Complete Herbal of 1652 recommends it both as food and medicine, and records from medieval monasteries document nettle soups, nettle puddings, and nettle-stuffed dishes as standard Lenten fare when preserved meats were forbidden. The plant's flavor, once blanched to neutralize its formic acid stingers, is remarkably complex: deeply green and herbaceous like spinach but with a more mineral, slightly nutty quality and an iron-rich depth that no cultivated green quite replicates. Nettles are among the most nutritionally dense wild plants available in temperate regions, containing significant iron, calcium, vitamins C and K, and a concentration of chlorophyll that turns any dish an extraordinary deep green.

Stinging nettles fell out of mainstream American culinary use as refrigeration, canning, and industrial agriculture made wild foraging feel unnecessary, but the ingredient has returned with vigor through the farm-to-table movement of the past two decades, championed by chefs who recognized in the nettle a flavor that cultivated greens cannot replicate. Farmers' markets in the Pacific Northwest, Northern California, and New England began offering nettle bunches each spring, and curious home cooks — armed with thick rubber gloves — discovered that the plant that had stung their ankles as children was actually delicious when treated with respect. On a burger, sautéed nettles function as a sophisticated alternative to the traditional lettuce leaf: they hold their structure under heat, they contribute a mineral, earthy depth that complements beef in a way that bland iceberg never could, and their striking dark green color against the crust of a medium-rare patty creates a visual drama that makes people want to know what they are eating before they've taken a bite.

I encountered nettles as a serious ingredient through a spring foraging walk I joined on a whim in the Cascade foothills of Washington State. Our guide, a botanist who also happened to cook professionally, filled a burlap bag with young nettle tops using gloved hands with the practiced ease of someone who had done it hundreds of times. Back at a camp kitchen she blanched them for ninety seconds in boiling salted water, squeezed them dry with a towel, and sautéed them in browned butter with nothing but garlic and a pinch of nutmeg. I ate them standing at the camp stove while she cooked, burning my tongue slightly because I couldn't wait, and the flavor hit me with the clean force of something wild and alive — green and mineral and faintly smoky from the butter and completely unlike anything I had grown in a garden. I spent the next spring with rubber gloves and a basket, gathering nettles from the edge of a creek bed near my apartment, and put them on a burger that same evening. It was right immediately, in the way that certain ingredient-protein combinations are simply inevitable once you encounter them.

The mineral, iron-forward intensity of sautéed stinging nettles is a topping that demands a properly cooked medium-rare patty to make sense. Nettles cooked correctly — blanched, squeezed dry, and sautéed in brown butter with garlic — carry a pronounced earthiness that pairs specifically with the sanguine, slightly bloody quality of medium-rare beef. On an overcooked patty the nettles taste aggressive and disconnected, the two strong flavors competing rather than collaborating. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit the medium-rare beef provides a rosy, rich, fatty counterpoint to the lean mineral green of the nettles, and the natural juices in the rested patty provide the liquid that allows the sautéed greens to relax into the burger rather than sit awkwardly on top of it. This is a burger for people who take both their beef and their greens seriously. Do not overcook the patty. The nettles know, and they will tell on you.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
2 tbsp mixed seeds (poppy, sesame, sunflower) for topping
400g fresh young stinging nettles (use gloves when handling), rinsed
Fine sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 tbsp blanched stinging nettles, squeezed dry and finely chopped
Fine sea salt and white pepper to taste
1 tbsp unsalted butter for finishing the nettles
2 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
instructions: 1. SAFETY NOTE for handling nettles: Always use thick rubber or latex gloves when handling fresh stinging nettles. Blanching completely neutralizes the sting.

2. Blanch the nettles: Bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil. Using gloved hands, add all the nettles and submerge them. Blanch for 60 to 90 seconds until wilted and bright dark green. Transfer immediately to an ice bath. Once cool, drain and use your hands (gloves no longer needed after blanching) to squeeze out as much water as possible. Roughly chop the blanched nettles.

3. Make the nettle-and-goat-cheese cream: Set aside a small portion (2 tbsp) of the finely chopped blanched nettles. Beat together goat cheese and cream cheese until smooth. Add the finely chopped nettles, lemon juice, garlic, and heavy cream. Mix until combined and creamy. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

4. Make the seeded whole-wheat buns: Combine both flours, yeast, salt, and honey in a stand mixer bowl. Add warm water and oil. Mix on low then increase to medium and knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky.

5. Cover and let rise 1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 portions, shape into rounds, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Proof covered 60 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with mixed seeds. Bake 18 to 20 minutes. Cool on a rack.
6. Make the garlic-herb mayo: Stir together mayonnaise, grated garlic, parsley, chives, and lemon juice. Season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Prepare patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 170g). Shape into 3/4-inch-thick patties with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with kosher salt, black pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.
8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side undisturbed.
9. Flip, immediately place a slice of Fontina or Gruyère on each patty. Tent with a dome or lid. Cook 90 seconds to 2 minutes more.
10. Check internal temperature — pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a rack for 3 minutes.

11. While patties rest, sauté the nettles: In a wide skillet over medium-high heat, melt butter until it begins to foam and turn golden brown (beurre noisette stage). Add sliced garlic and sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant but not brown. Add the blanched chopped nettles and toss vigorously to coat in the brown butter.

12. Season with nutmeg, salt, and black pepper. Cook for 2 minutes until heated through and any remaining moisture has evaporated. Finish with a squeeze of lemon juice and the extra tablespoon of butter for gloss. Keep warm.
13. Split buns and toast cut-side down in a pan over medium heat for 60 to 90 seconds.
14. Assemble: Spread the nettle-and-goat-cheese cream generously on the bottom bun.
15. Place the rested cheese-topped patty on top. Immediately pile a generous mound of sautéed nettles over the cheese.
16. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Spread garlic-herb mayo on the inside of the top bun, close the burger, and serve at once.
